purpose: Filgrastim helps your body make more white blood cells, especially a type called neutrophils that fight infections. It is often used after chemotherapy, bone marrow transplant, or in people whose bodies do not make enough white blood cells on their own. It helps lower your risk of getting serious infections when your immune system is weak.
how_it_works: Your body naturally makes a protein called G-CSF that tells your bone marrow to produce infection-fighting white blood cells. Filgrastim is a man-made version of that same protein. When you get this medication, it signals your bone marrow to ramp up production and release more white blood cells into your bloodstream to help protect you.
common_side_effects: Bone or muscle aches and pain (especially in the lower back, hips, or legs) are very common and usually manageable with over-the-counter pain relievers. You may also experience redness, soreness, or bruising at the injection site, headache, tiredness, nausea, or a mild fever.
warnings: Rarely, filgrastim can cause a serious condition called Splenic Rupture (a burst spleen), so call your doctor right away if you have sudden sharp pain in your upper left belly or left shoulder. It can also cause a serious lung reaction called ARDS, so tell your doctor immediately if you have sudden shortness of breath or trouble breathing. People with sickle cell disease need close monitoring because it can trigger a sickle cell crisis. Also alert your doctor if you notice unusual swelling, decreased urination, or signs of an allergic reaction like hives or facial swelling.
typical_dosing: Filgrastim is given as an injection, either under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (IV). The dose depends on why you are taking it, your weight, and your medical condition. A typical starting dose is around 5 micrograms per kilogram of body weight per day. Your doctor or nurse will determine the right dose and schedule for you, and they will check your blood counts regularly to adjust the dose as needed.
